From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article should list *only* official names approved by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU).[[1]](#cite_note-IAU-USGS-1)

* Mercurian: 414 craters (7.9%)
* Lunar: 1,624 craters (31.1%)
* Martian: 1,092 craters (20.9%)
* Venusian: 900 craters (17.2%)
* Others: 1,198 craters (22.9%)

Distribution of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") as of 2017[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit)[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

This is a list of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"), the [innermost planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_planets "Inner planets") of the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") *(for other features, see [list of geological features on Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_geological_features_on_Mercury "List of geological features on Mercury"))*.[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) Most Mercurian craters [are named after](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_nomenclature "Planetary nomenclature") famous writers, artists and composers. According to the rules by IAU's [Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_Group_for_Planetary_System_Nomenclature "Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature"), all new craters must be named after an artist that was famous for more than fifty years, and dead for more than three years, before the date they are named.[[6]](#cite_note-Ritzel-7) Craters larger than 250 km in diameter are referred to as "basins" *(also see [§ Terminology](#Terminology))*.[[7]](#cite_note-8)[[8]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-9)

As of 2025[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit), there are 444 named Mercurian craters,[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) a small fraction of the total number of named Solar System craters, most of which are [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon"), [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars") and [Venerian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Venus "List of craters on Venus") craters.[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)") ([141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Callisto "List of craters on Callisto")), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") ([131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Ganymede "List of craters on Ganymede")), [Rhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhea_(moon) "Rhea (moon)") (128), [Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta "4 Vesta") (90), [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (90), [Dione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dione_(moon) "Dione (moon)") (73), [Iapetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (58), [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_(moon) "Enceladus (moon)") (53), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(moon) "Tethys (moon)") (50) and [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)") ([41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Europa "List of craters on Europa")). For a full list, *see [List of craters in the Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_in_the_Solar_System "List of craters in the Solar System")*.

# Dr. Seuss, Alvin Ailey among the Names Selected for 23 Mercury Craters

Apr 26, 2012

The International Astronomical Union (IAU) recently approved a proposal from the MESSENGER Science Team to assign 23 new names to impact craters on Mercury. The IAU has been the arbiter of planetary and satellite nomenclature since its inception in 1919. In keeping with the established naming theme for craters on Mercury, all of the newly designated features are named after famous deceased artists, musicians, or authors.

# Visit to a Small, Cold Planet

Ancient Romans named Mercury for their messenger of the gods

![Mercury's craters (NASA/Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory/Carnegie Institution of Washington)](https://theamericanscholar.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/04/mercury_nasa.jpg "mercury_nasa")

It’s out there spinning, tied by gravity’s leash to the sun. Round and round it runs, a small planet vacillating between freezing and burning according to whether it’s night or day. Mercury’s temperatures can fall to -290 Fahrenheit at night, and can rise to 800 degrees Fahrenheit by day. That day is, according to NASA, 175.97 Earth days long. Long day’s journey into night.

It’s one of the four terrestrial planets and it’s the planet closest to the [sun](https://theamericanscholar.org/tetelestai "A Great Event"). It’s slightly larger than Earth’s [moon](https://theamericanscholar.org/the-moon-2/ "The Moon"), with a landscape smacked and pocked by craters, which are impact scars of comets and meteoroids. The thin atmosphere is too thin to burn them up upon entry. These are old craters.

Volcanoes to coat old craters with hot lava are also lacking. Volcanoes died out early in Mercury’s history. Because it’s so small, its hot core cooled off during its first billion years. The cooling-off process caused the planet to contract, which is likely why Mercury has tremendous cliffs whose faces rise straight up to nearly a mile high. In the contracting and crumbling of the crust, some parts were left sticking up.

Mercury has a big basin, Caloris Basin, almost a thousand miles in diameter, made by an immense asteroid impact a long time ago. The planet’s orbit traces the shape of an egg, so that its distance from the sun varies from 29 million to 43 million miles. If you were to stand on Mercury at perihelion (when its orbit veers closest to the Sun), you would see our Sun three times as big as we see it from here.

Another thing about Mercury, it has ice on its poles, deep within craters, ice probably delivered by comets.

The ancient Romans named the planet Mercury for their messenger god. In 2008 and 2009, NASA’s Messenger spacecraft performed three flybys of Mercury. In March 2011 the planet’s gravity helped pull the Messenger into orbit, where it remains.

The god Mercury was the Roman version of  Hermes of ancient Greece. Hermes was a stealer of cattle, a player of the lyre, a cooker-up of tricky schemes, a trickster, a border crosser from light to dark and back to light. (I’m reading Lewis Hyde’s translation of the “Homeric Hymn to Hermes.”)

If you want the richest, most tantalizing, most complex, most profound, most engrossing ramble through the spiritual and psychological world of that mercurial figure, the trickster (now that we’ve moved from the planet Mercury to its namesake), try *Trickster Makes This World* by Lewis Hyde. Many of us will live without ever seeing Mercury (the planet is too close to the sun to see most of the time, though it’s visible at sunset). But to live without ever experiencing Lewis Hyde’s book on its namesake—that would be sad.

[Priscilla Long](https://theamericanscholar.org/author/priscilla-long/)’s latest book is *Cartographies of Home: Poems.* Forthcoming is a collection of essays, *On Spaces and Colors.* She is author of two other books of poetry, a book on thriving while aging, a collection of memoirist essays titled *Fire and Stone,* the how-to guides *Minding the Muse: A Handbook for Painters, Composers, Writers, and Other Creators* and *The Writer’s Portable Mentor,* as well as *Where the Sun Never Shines: A History of America’s Bloody Coal Industry.*

**Hemingway** is a [crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"). It has a patch of very dark material located near its center. The dark color is likely due to rocks that have a different mineralogical composition from that of the surrounding surface.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

The crater's name was adopted by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU) in 2009. It is named for the American author [Ernest Hemingway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernest_Hemingway "Ernest Hemingway").[[2]](#cite_note-2)

The small crater [Makeba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Makeba_(crater) "Makeba (crater)") is southeast of Hemingway.

## Dark interior crater

The dark depression near the center of Hemingway is truly black, and due to its superposition over the other structures in the crater, it is a young feature. The dark material is probably abundant in the subsurface of the crater and is being exposed by [mass wasting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_wasting "Mass wasting") processes and the formation of [hollows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollows_(Mercury) "Hollows (Mercury)").[[3]](#cite_note-3) The irregular depression itself may have formed by explosive volcanism.[[4]](#cite_note-Thomas-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5) There is an unnamed crater to the southeast of Hemingway that may also be the site of explosive volcanism.[[4]](#cite_note-Thomas-4)

**Faulkner** is a crater on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"). It has a diameter of 168 kilometres (104 miles). Its name was adopted by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU) on April 24, 2012. Faulkner is named for the American author [William Faulkner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Faulkner "William Faulkner").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Faulkner is part of [Apārangi Planitia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apārangi_Planitia "Apārangi Planitia"), a flat plain extending to the south and west of the crater. Immediately to the east of Faulkner is an unnamed [peak ring basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_ring "Peak ring"), one of 110 on Mercury.[[2]](#cite_note-2) Further to the southeast is another peak ring crater, [Caravaggio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caravaggio_(crater) "Caravaggio (crater)").

# Frost (crater)

**Frost** is a [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_craters "Lunar craters") [impact crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") that is attached to the southern rim [Landau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landau_(crater) "Landau (crater)"), a [walled plain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walled_plain "Walled plain") on the [far side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Far_side_(Moon) "Far side (Moon)") of the [Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon "Moon").[[1]](#cite_note-Moore_2000-1) Just to the east is [Petropavlovskiy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petropavlovskiy_(crater) "Petropavlovskiy (crater)"), and to the northeast along the edge of Landau is [Razumov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Razumov_(crater) "Razumov (crater)"). The crater [Douglass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglass_(lunar_crater) "Douglass (lunar crater)") is located less than a crater diameter to the west-southwest.

The outer rim of Frost is eroded, but is overlaid by only one small craterlet along the northeast side. The inner wall is wider and heavier along the northern side where it has been reinforced by the former rim of Landau. The northern part of the interior floor is occupied by two smaller craters, with the larger of the two along the northwest inner wall. The southern part of the floor is relatively level and featureless.

Prior to formal naming by the [IAU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") in 1970,[[2]](#cite_note-2) Frost was called *Crater 166*.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

**Ellington** is a [crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)") named after [Duke Ellington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_Ellington "Duke Ellington"), an American composer, pianist, and leader of a jazz orchestra. It was named by the [IAU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") in 2012.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Ellington is one of 110 [peak ring basins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_ring "Peak ring") on Mercury.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

Within Ellington is the smaller crater [Berkel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berkel_(crater) "Berkel (crater)"). The somewhat smaller crater [Derain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derain_(crater) "Derain (crater)") is to the northwest. Both Derain and Ellington lie within a much older, 730-km-diameter, unnamed crater (referred to as b36).[[3]](#cite_note-3) The crater [Nasir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_(crater) "Nasir (crater)") is to the south of Ellington.

**Ellington** is a [crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)") named after [Duke Ellington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_Ellington "Duke Ellington"), an American composer, pianist, and leader of a jazz orchestra. It was named by the [IAU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") in 2012.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Ellington is one of 110 [peak ring basins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_ring "Peak ring") on Mercury.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

Within Ellington is the smaller crater [Berkel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berkel_(crater) "Berkel (crater)"). The somewhat smaller crater [Derain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derain_(crater) "Derain (crater)") is to the northwest. Both Derain and Ellington lie within a much older, 730-km-diameter, unnamed crater (referred to as b36).[[3]](#cite_note-3) The crater [Nasir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_(crater) "Nasir (crater)") is to the south of Ellington.

**Ellington** is a [crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)") named after [Duke Ellington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_Ellington "Duke Ellington"), an American composer, pianist, and leader of a jazz orchestra. It was named by the [IAU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") in 2012.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Ellington is one of 110 [peak ring basins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_ring "Peak ring") on Mercury.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

Within Ellington is the smaller crater [Berkel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berkel_(crater) "Berkel (crater)"). The somewhat smaller crater [Derain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derain_(crater) "Derain (crater)") is to the northwest. Both Derain and Ellington lie within a much older, 730-km-diameter, unnamed crater (referred to as b36).[[3]](#cite_note-3) The crater [Nasir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_(crater) "Nasir (crater)") is to the south of Ellington.

**Brooks** is a [crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on the southwestern part [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"). It has a diameter of 34 kilometers. Its name was adopted by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") in 2015, and refers to the American poet and novelist [Gwendolyn Brooks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gwendolyn_Brooks "Gwendolyn Brooks") (1917–2000).[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Brooks is east of the large crater [Dostoevskij](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dostoevskij_(crater) "Dostoevskij (crater)").

**Copland** is an [impact crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"). Its floor is flooded with volcanic smooth plains material, which could be related to the activity that formed the nearby bright vent known as [Nathair Facula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathair_Facula "Nathair Facula").

## Naming

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Copland_(crater)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Naming")]

Amateur astronomer Ronald Dantowitz and his colleagues Scott Teare and Marek Kozubal used the Mt. Wilson 60-inch telescope in 1998 to observe a very bright feature on this portion of Mercury's surface, and they assumed that the bright feature was an impact crater. Mr. Dantowitz expressed his wish that the crater be named "Copland" (after American composer [Aaron Copland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Copland "Aaron Copland")) once better images of the area were obtained from spacecraft.

Surprisingly, *[MESSENGER](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MESSENGER "MESSENGER")* images from Mercury flyby 3 revealed that the small bright feature, seen at the left edge of this image and now known as [Nathair Facula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathair_Facula "Nathair Facula"), is not an [impact crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") but more closely resembles a [volcanic vent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanic_vent "Volcanic vent"). No convention for naming volcanic vents on Mercury had yet been adopted, because none were identified prior to *MESSENGER*'s first Mercury flyby. A *MESSENGER* team member corresponded with Mr. Dantowitz and suggested that the name Copland be proposed instead for a large crater nearby. He agreed, and the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU) approved the name Copland on March 3, 2010.[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-IAU-2)

**Joplin** is a crater on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"). Its name was adopted by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU) in 2012, after the American composer [Scott Joplin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Joplin "Scott Joplin").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Joplin's [peak ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_ring "Peak ring") is relatively small compared to the crater diameter and it is offset from the center. It is one of 110 peak ring basins on Mercury.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

Joplin is located about half-way between the prominent crater [Debussy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debussy_(crater) "Debussy (crater)") and the crater [Lennon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lennon_(crater) "Lennon (crater)"). It is south of the crater [Travers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travers_(crater) "Travers (crater)"). Together with crater [Bulsara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulsara_(crater) "Bulsara (crater)") (named after [Freddie Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Mercury "Freddie Mercury")), Lennon and Joplin form a line of nearly equally spaced craters.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

**Joplin** is a crater on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"). Its name was adopted by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU) in 2012, after the American composer [Scott Joplin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Joplin "Scott Joplin").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Joplin's [peak ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_ring "Peak ring") is relatively small compared to the crater diameter and it is offset from the center. It is one of 110 peak ring basins on Mercury.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

Joplin is located about half-way between the prominent crater [Debussy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debussy_(crater) "Debussy (crater)") and the crater [Lennon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lennon_(crater) "Lennon (crater)"). It is south of the crater [Travers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travers_(crater) "Travers (crater)"). Together with crater [Bulsara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulsara_(crater) "Bulsara (crater)") (named after [Freddie Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Mercury "Freddie Mercury")), Lennon and Joplin form a line of nearly equally spaced craters.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

**Seuss** is a crater on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"). Its name was adopted by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU) in 2012. It is named for the American author and cartoonist Theodor Seuss Geisel, better known as [Dr. Seuss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dr._Seuss "Dr. Seuss").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Seuss is one of the largest craters of the [Kuiperian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_Mercury "Geology of Mercury") system on Mercury. The largest is [Bartók](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bartók_(crater) "Bartók (crater)") crater.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

[Hollows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollows_(Mercury) "Hollows (Mercury)") are present within Seuss.

The *Acadia Rupes* is an escarpment located west of Seuss.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

**Seuss** is a crater on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"). Its name was adopted by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU) in 2012. It is named for the American author and cartoonist Theodor Seuss Geisel, better known as [Dr. Seuss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dr._Seuss "Dr. Seuss").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Seuss is one of the largest craters of the [Kuiperian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_Mercury "Geology of Mercury") system on Mercury. The largest is [Bartók](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bartók_(crater) "Bartók (crater)") crater.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

[Hollows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollows_(Mercury) "Hollows (Mercury)") are present within Seuss.

The *Acadia Rupes* is an escarpment located west of Seuss.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

**Ives** is a crater on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)").[[1]](#cite_note-1) Its name was adopted by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU) in 1979. Ives is named for the American composer [Charles Ives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Ives "Charles Ives"), who lived from 1874 to 1954.[[2]](#cite_note-2) The crater was first imaged by [Mariner 10](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariner_10 "Mariner 10") in 1974.[[3]](#cite_note-Davies_1978-3)

Ives has a bright [ray system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_system "Ray system").

Ives is northeast of [Surikov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surikov_(crater) "Surikov (crater)") crater and north of [Michelangelo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelangelo_(crater) "Michelangelo (crater)").
